blocks.x: . He might have a singer.
I was thinking about that.
Wait, what's the date of today? Today's the November what? The 11th?
The 13th, isn't it?

Already? Oh my God. 13th of November 1975. Let me get some papers together. And there's an interview with Henry Roland Byrd. And what are we going to talk about? See, Fester, something I always wanted to ask you. I know you were born in Bugaloosa up there. And you said you'd moved here to New Orleans.
Yeah, he brought me here when I was about two months old.
Yeah. What did your father do?
I never even knew what my daddy did. My mother raised me.
Yeah, so you don't? No, I didn't. What was his name?
James Lucius Byrd.
James Lucius?
Lucius. Yeah, Byrd.
Did his family, he came from Bugaloosa like your mother?
No, I don't really know where he came from, really. He just... He was never in my life.
Oh, so you never knew him?
I never knew him that well. Did...
Did... And what was your mother's name? My mother was named Ella Mae Bird. Ella Mae. Ella Mae.

Ella Mae Bird. Where? She was from Bugaloosa? No, she was born in... Brookhaven, Mississippi. Mm-hmm. And she met your father in Bugaloosa? I think she met him in Macomb somewhere. See, he played music too. What?
Do you know what did she meet?
No, really I don't. I really don't. Like I said, I don't know too much about him, you know, at all.
But how many people in your family played music? Did anybody else? Any of your relatives?
So on that paper we got from your uncle, said your grandfather was America's Bird. Who? America's Bird.
Yeah.
Your grandfather.
Grandfather was America's? America's Bird?
America's Bird.
Like America, but America's?
Yeah. But it said on that paper when he was born and where he was born.
Yeah, on the... Yeah, I didn't know he was going to ask me these questions.
I forgot. I forgot. It's way back. Give me a change.
I've got it.
Give me a change. I want to go get the signal.
Yeah, I got the signal.
Thank you, doctor. You want anything?
No, I don't want anything. Coke. That's all right. Oh, okay. Who knows? So you said you came to hear what? Right after you were born? I mean, two years after you were born?
Well, as I was told, my mother said she brought me here when I was about two months old.
Yeah. Mm-hmm. And who else was in your family? You had any brothers and sisters? Well, I had one brother, as I know, Robert Burrett.
He died. He died. He died. I was away when he died. I don't know exactly what he is. He died here.
Mm-hmm. He was older or younger than you? He was older than I was. But by a couple years?
No, I'd say he was about eight or nine years old when I was.
Oh, then your mother and father must have been married for a while. Yeah. Before you came along?
Yeah, they were.
So once you...
They separated after I was born, about two months after I was born, when she split, you know.
Mm-hmm. So once you moved to New Orleans, what neighborhood did you live in?
Did we live in then? We lived in the area between Howard Avenue and Canal, around in Drys and Ramport. Yeah. Girard.
Just right around the section. You were a downtown person.
Yeah.
You weren't really uptown. Yeah, really. Were there any musicians who lived in that neighborhood? Do you remember any? In the downtown neighborhood? Yeah. Around where you were living?
Well, really, you don't never know where the musicians be living at. I mean, they just all gather, drift around, and they get to the right places where they can enjoy one another, you know.
Was there any clubs in your neighborhood?

Yeah, we had a special club that they had, rather. I was real small. I was just learning then. What was the name of it? At that time, the club name was, they called it Caleoca and Franklin, but it was Del P's Club. Del P's Club? Del P's, yeah.
It was at Caleoca and Franklin. Yeah. But it's not Franklin Avenue anymore. No. It's another name? Yeah, Franklin and I, Loyola, yeah.
Yeah, it's Loyola in there. It's a lot of streets being cut out.
Yeah, because they changed a lot of streets up in there.
Yeah, because, see, right in the middle of Howard Avenue was the old basin.
Right.
The basin. Ran through there all the way to the lake.
Right.
Well, all that's been filled in.
Yeah, well, yeah, I know, because they used to have a train that went out to the lake. That's right. But after the war, when they filled all that new land in for those houses out there.
They had big ships and boats and all. They used to come up in the basin. Okay.
Wait, it was in this neighborhood that you would hear musicians, in other words, up in this?
Yeah, Louis Armstrong was familiar with us around in this neighborhood. Where he stayed I don't know. But I mean he was up in the neighborhood. Yeah, in that neighborhood.
That was his hunting grounds.
Jack Dupree and Father Toots as you all call it now. Yeah, yeah. Big Bramble, well he's dead now. He played trumpet. Junior, Little Junior they called him, he played drums.
What was Little Junior's name? Do you remember? No. Big Bramble's name?
No, I really don't know. All I knew his name was Little Junior.
You just knew it by those names? Yeah, Little Junior, or Big Bramble.
And they had Sonny Boy Williams.
Yeah, well Sonny Boy would come in every now and then.
Yeah, he'd come back up to the Forks when he'd leave, that's where he would come back to.
Now he'd play at this club you mentioned?
The LPs, everybody played music then.
So it was kind of a club for drifters, a lot of people drifted in, and locals. Yeah, locals, towers, yeah. So it was not only jazz would be played there, but a lot of blues.
Any kind of music that we could play, yeah.
Would you play there? Blues, pop, rumba, anything? Yep.
Just anything that you could play, you were welcome to play it.
Was there an owner, somebody ran the club?
Yeah, Del P owned the place. That was the guy's name? That was the guy's name. That's why they called it Del P's. Del P's. And them that didn't know his name was C. Caliokin Franklin.
Oh, so it was sort of a pseudonym for the club. Yeah, it was in between, yeah. Well, did, so that was the hangout spot?
That was the original hangout spot, because you could get work there, you see. People would hear you there and hire you on other places.
Was this, when you first started playing music, do you remember when you first started?
Well I started hanging out around there listening to all of those people. I was real small. I was a minor, rather, you know. I wasn't allowed to go in the bar rooms at that time.
Were the cops hanging out around there? Well, sometimes, you know.
A lot of trouble? Cops wasn't too bad, no bader than they is now. They get off their base sometimes.
Yeah, yeah, but I mean, you know, it was a heavy club with a lot of fights and things. Well, you had lots of those, you know. Because that was a tough area, I know. Really, really.
I would hate to imagine to go back there now. Yeah, go back there now.
Downtown's always been bad, you know. That section. I mean, the whole downtown area, you know. It didn't play in that time. Yeah, yeah. It was a popcorn kid.
No, no, no, no. German. There is a Coca-Cola. German.
German Coca-Cola. German Coca-Cola. You know you're right. It's good.
You know you're right.
What?
Beer. German Coca-Cola. Yeah. They drink good beer in Germany. No, they do.
Some of the best. I think the best. In the world. What's some of the best beer? Yeah. Yeah. They drink good beer in Germany.
They drink good beer in Germany. No, they do.
Some of the best.
I think the best in the world.
What's some of the first music you listened to? Did you learn any, you must have learned some religious music. Did your mother teach you any music? Yeah.
My mother taught me practically everything I knew. About all music? About music. Drum, piano, bass, guitar, dancing. Did you sing?
So your first contact with music was through your mother and it was? Through my mother, yeah. What kind of, spirituals or?

I played whatever she played. She played any little thing, you know, spiritual. What kind of solace? She played balance, she played sentimental. My mother was a professional musician. Oh, she played for money?
She played by music. Yeah, she played for money.
She could read?
I mean she could read music? Yeah. Did she teach you to read or did you ever get that job?
I tried but I didn't like to read a part of it, you know. I liked to play, get down with it. Yeah, yeah, yeah. What the boys was doing around the corner.
But you did do church playing before. Yeah. I heard you say one time when you went to the joint to start playing, that you had been playing

a lot. Yeah I played a lot of music on guitar. Wait, now what was your? I do most of the music, religious on the guitar. I have tried a lot of times, you know what I mean, to capture it on the piano, but I'm a little bit better with guitar on religious tunes than I am on rhythm and blues.
So what was the first instrument that you played though?

Let me give you a short dissertation. I played the trunk. Wait a second. I'll give you a short dissertation on the evolution of his rhythms into his music. The first instrument he played with this, the bottom of his feet, when he was earning a weapon as a tap dancer. And he worked his rhythms out. Wait, wait, wait. Let me ask him that.
Wait, let me just tell you a little thing. Okay.
He worked his, you don't want to know what to ask. He worked his rhythms out first on his feet as a tap dancer.
Worked out his rhythms on his feet as a tap dancer.

Wait a second. Let me tell you what I'm going to tell you. Okay. So he was dancing and some other cats was playing. And what he was playing on his feet was the first expression of like the kind of rhythms that's in it. What he played on his feet. And then he started playing drums in the little band. He'd get like orange crates and like from the movie house, those metal cans that they put the film in and make sounds out of. Right. He started playing drums and the rhythms that was in his body that he played on his feet, he transferred them to the drums. So when he went into piano he had to-
Transferred the drums?

No, he had to teach the drummers that he got how to play because he learned his things on the drums from his feet. Then that's why he became the professor because he was teaching the drummers how to play his rhythms so they could back him up on piano. Right. Because the only way he could play piano was to teach a drummer what to play.
So he had to teach the drummers- What to do. What to do.
Oh yeah.
That's pretty good. I'm going to ask him the same- Now I'm going to ask him the same thing. Come on. I do. No, I got some things here man. Don't go- You're missing my show.
Did you- Oh, is this your show? No.

Come on, Quint. Don't be hard with me. Y'all being hard with me. Wait a minute. Okay, we're going to- Did you know all that? Basically, yeah. I'd figured that out. Not- not specifically all that, but almost. So, alright. I'm- So you said- So what was your first- your first instrument? Was it- Was it a drumming or was it your first real instrument? Was it Quint- uh, Fess? What was your first instrument? The first instrument that you played? That I played? Yeah. Real instrument? Instrument, yeah. Guitar. Guitar. Was it a box guitar or- It was a regular uh-
Acoustic? Acoustic guitar? Not acoustic. They didn't have electric guitars then.
Yeah, I know then.
The acoustic, yeah.
Now how far did you get? I mean how good were you?
Well I didn't really- it irritated my fingers a lot. I mean I could play one or two-
It always does when you- but how- did you play? You learned four chords or you could play a couple chords?
Well I could play the whole- I could play the whole chord though. I could play four, six, eight. I could play in C very well.
And the key of C is your best?

Yeah. Well I was on my way of using a choker at that time. You can change the keyboard with the choker. Yeah, with the choker. But somewhere down the line I figured it was too much of trouble. You know to try to keep up with guitar. At that time you had to buy strings and all of them were popping. The guitar wasn't as strong as they is now. It was always something going around.
What kind of guitar? Was it a cheap guitar? Like from Sears or was it an expensive guitar? Yeah, it was really cheap. Yeah, wasn't it-
It wasn't much bigger than the ukulele. Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, I know that kind. It's something to try to make a hustle with.
So what was the first time you tried to form a group? Was there a point where you tried to form a group? You know, first really get out and perform in front of people.

In front of people? Well, I got a chance to do that with, uh, well, we was working at the Cotton Club. We had a mixed group then. Let me see who was with us. We had Jack Dupreak with us then, because Jack Dupreak was singing in the community then. He wasn't playing music. I learned him a little bit about the piano and he learned me a little bit about the blues and singing lines. So we just transferred one thing to the other.
Right.
So you would teach each other.
You'd show him something, he'd show you something.

So the guy at the Cotton Club bought a piano. And, uh, I had been banging on the pianos and people at home and places and listening, like I see these clubs. So I figured I was good enough to take a chance in there because there wasn't nothing really happening no harm. Where was the Cotton Club? That was on Ramport between, uh, Caliope and Clio. Really? You had most of your big time clubs then. Around 37, 38, 39, most of your clubs was around in between Caliope and Clio on Ramport. You had the Cotton Club, you had the Dixie Bell, you had the Porter's Inn. You had a few little joints on the other side of the street. I can't remember the names right now.
Can I ask you a question? Mm-hmm. Where did Big Joe Turner play?
Now, Turner played the Rhythm Club, didn't he? At the Dewdrop most of the time. Dewdrop in the Rhythm Club. Yeah.
What years was that? 48, 47.
Yeah, that's way back in the years. 47 and 80 years. You know what he's doing now?
Turner's out on the coast, I know.

Could I bring him for the festival? I heard he was, he was, he was drinking a lot. Yeah. And I heard from Norbert Hess that he was just getting over it and it's possible. But it might not be possible.
Norbert has to know how to get in touch with him?

Yeah, right, Norbert. Norbert should know how to get in touch with him. He told me he had seen him. Thank you. And I don't know exactly all the details. So after, you know, after you, what was, so the first group you got was with Dupree. You went in.

Not my group, I was just with them. I worked with them. That's the first showing that I appeared with in the public. Mm-hmm. I was with them. Sonny Boyd Williams, we worked together at the New York Inn. Well I made appearance in front of people. Nothing professional.
Yeah, this is just amateur stuff.

Yeah. To make a quarter, you know. First group that I formed was Al Miller. With Al Miller. Yeah. Robert Parker. One size. One that recorded Balfootin'. Yeah. And myself. It was hard to go way back. I had another kid with me with a- Swish? No, this was a different thing. This was the very first group that I formed. And I came to, I can't think of his name, but he was a little, he certainly looked like a little Hungarian boy. He wasn't from here, you know. What about, wouldn't Walter Nelson with you?
Not at that time.

That's why I named the band. That's the other kid that I'm trying to call his name, I can't remember it off hand now. We did knew that he was- Hungarian? He was a Hungarian. He claimed to be a Hungarian, you know. So that's why I named my band.
Well he was white then. Professor Longhair.
No, he wasn't white.
He was black and he claimed to be a Hungarian? He wasn't really black, he. Oh, so he was sort of-
Yeah.
One of those kind of- Oh, so that's why you called the band-

Shefflin Hungarians. Because he was really a- Hungarian. He was a cat to work with, you know. Giving me inspiration. What did he play? He played bongos and congos and played the sticks. And tambourines and- Combs and juice pop.

So he was an extra percussionist? Oh yeah, he played a little, every little thing. Well, let's get back to the- So you first started dancing, you said? Yeah. So that was before you really got into the music. Yeah. So who'd you first dance with? Who were the people you danced with? You must have had a group that you danced with.

Well, we streamlined Isaac. Streamline who? Streamline Isaac. At that time, he used to go off a lot. And he'd learn all of these different dances and things. And when he'd come back, he would teach them to me.
Now who- Where would he go out of town? Yeah, he was traveling.
He'd be around us today, right today. Maybe sometime I'd get him together and he'll, you know, give you an interview. I thought-
Wasn't there somebody named Streamline Harris?
Streamline Isaac Harris Isidore. All of those are his name. Isidore Isaac Harris. His full name was Streamline Isaac Harris.
He's around. Isidore. That's his full name? He's still around. Wow. Yeah, he's still around.
Because he's a little fat now. Oh no.
Yeah, we probably can't dance.
Who else was in the group? Wasn't there? Well, what he would teach me, I would teach a friend of mine, call him Hike, Harrison Hike.
Harrison Hike?
You might have heard him.
Yeah, I've heard of Harrison Hike.

So we three, when he would come back, we three would do a Clark step like you said, the Austin Brothers does, if you ever listen to him, or Bill Robinson. Yeah, yeah. We used to do all of these kind of things, you know. I had other little acts I would put in it. Streamline was an acrobat, and he taught me a little, you know, little tricks to the tree. I used to run up the wall, so high, three or four feet up a wall and turn around and come back down.
Did you do any jump through tumble salts or something, that kind of thing? Yeah.
Over one another's back, through one another's leg, over the table.
So where would you all perform in town?
Well like I say we performed around Cotton Club, Poles Inn, New York Inn.
Did you do any of the big theaters? I mean I know Lincoln Theater was open at that time. Did you perform at the Lincoln?
Yeah, at the Lincoln, during the time I played at the Palace of Lincoln I was playing music then. I switched from dancing. But we used to dance all up and down Bourbon.
Would you dance for money, on the street for money?
That's what the idea is. Well they still do that. Yeah.
You see that guy in Bourbon Street? I forget his name. There's some guy, he's great.
Is that guy in Port Shop? Ah, that might be him. His name is Isaac Mason.
What's his name in a couple of days? He's great. Yeah, I was never even seen him.
You find your best dancers out there. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
He's really terrific. So you were, did you ever, somebody said you played a minstrel show once. You used to work in a minstrel show.

Well I was real small. I wasn't doing anything then. I was just trying to make a buck. And they'd use me as a kick stunt man. You know, whenever they had some water to pull on somebody, a pie to batten your feet. That was my job. Wait, did you go out of town with these people on the road? No, I never went nowhere. That was the CJK medicine. CJK? Yeah, that was the name of the medicine the cat was selling. And then something like the Hattie Cole.

So the name of the, the name of the, the. The minstrel show. The minstrel show was CJK. Yeah, minstrel show. The c period, j period, k period. Yeah. CJK. And that was the, so that was the name of the minstrel show and the stuff he was selling.
Yeah, that was the name of the medicine that he was selling would kill anything. He claimed. Yeah.
It wouldn't do. So you got tired of that? You didn't like what they were.
Well, lollipops. I don't know whether you heard of him. Lollipop. Yeah, lollipop Jones. Lollipop Jones in Memphis. Memphis, uh, Lewis. Lewis. Memphis Lewis.

Oh, you know some shit. Oh man, I told you, I could come into these things, you gotta know some things, you know? You know, just, uh, come in here and scare them, you know? I know, but I've been in a while to interviews with him and you know some shit nobody else knows. I know, you don't think I'm gonna come in here half-cum.
I don't know.
I'm paying for this, man.
I like that, man.
I'm already light. Okay, so when you meet, now Lollipop was a great comedian. He was. You must have learned a lot from him. He was. He was great. I mean, I know I've seen, I know.
Between him and Red Fox.
Yeah, him and Red Fox. You met Red Fox? He used to work with us.
Dewdrop.
At the Dewdrop. Yeah, I'll bet Red Fox did. All those comedians came to the Dewdrop.
Yeah, a pleasure work with him.

All those comedians came, I'll bet. Yeah. All the great comedians of the 50s, black comedians, all came to the Dewdrop. You know Scoey Mitchell? Scoey Mitchell used to work at the Dewdrop. You didn't know that, huh? Yeah. Started out, we used to work for a long time at the Dewdrop. But anyway, we'll get back to you. That's where Roy Brown. Yeah, Roy Brown and all of us, everybody was at the Dewdrop. So what about, so you met, so this was before you were doing music, you met Lollipop?
Yeah, oh yeah, way before I was a small kid.
What year was this when you said you went with the Minstrel Show? Oh, I was small.
I was around seven, eight years old, delivering papers and shining shoes and running on the air.
So this must have been 19, about 1925 or so?
Somewhere around there, 25, 26, somewhere down there.
And then when you started tap dancing with, uh... I was around about 13, 14 years old. That could have been more, about 1932 or so, sometime in there. Had to be.

35, well, I remember then I was beginning to start wanting to play music. And then broke in, around 37 I went to the CC camp. CC camp, what was that? Yeah, I came, well that's how, it's three C's, that's how we go, Algecultras. Oh, I can't pronounce the name right off hand. But take, at the time, what was it going to call it? The CCC camp, three C's. And maybe later on you'll find out where it represented. Probably Civil Construction Corps, Civil Corps.
It was. Something with WPA?

Cooperation, yeah. What, you were working? So was it... Oh, that's what the idea was. What did you do? Did everything. We were planting trees, digging spillweeds, we were grading, we were sloping, we were building banks, we was cutting soil, we were laying soils. Yeah. We were opening up spillweeds, grading roads, putting gravel down, cutting trees if necessary. Yeah. Cleaning all the land.

Was this outside the city? Was this outside New Orleans? Yeah, just around Sweetport, all around Hardin. With all these people you worked, did you ever travel a great deal or did you just mostly stay around New Orleans?
Well, at CCC camp there was a lot of traveling in it.
Yeah.
You know what I mean? You never know where you're going until you get there. It's like a road crew. How did those things pay?
Did they, a dollar a day? What were they? Well, at that time I was getting fifty dollars a month. Oh yeah.

But if you had a dependent, well then they would send you a dependent fifty dollars a month and they would give you twenty-two, maybe twenty-eight, over there, where you was, where you were serving your time. And out of that you'd have to pay your laundry bills and, well you buy a canteen book, it's like you would spend checks and things out here, you bought canteen books in there and it represented money you know. So some guys I mean had other hustles in there besides that, which I did.
Did you play music while you were up to entertain the people?

Well the guy that was in charge of the company found out that I could play, and he got a piano from somewhere and put it in a recreation hall for me to entertain the soldiers so they would, you know, have something to do and somewhere to go. Well we'd knock off. Well I guess so I didn't have to drill much no more. Oh so this was, you were in the army? You were in the army?
Well you can consider it the army.
It was considered it.
Oh I thought it was some type of civilian work thing. Well this was all through, it was under the army.
It was under the army. Rules, regulations, yeah. So you were. We sold it, yeah, we drilled, we did everything a soldier would do, all the things, we had working periods too, you know.
So this was all through the late 30s? This was in 37. Till how long did this last?
Well I stayed in there six months. Oh so this was? My time was up. Seemed like six years.
Probably did.
Really, with that work going on I wasn't expecting that. And you had to study, you had to go to school, you had to drill, and a whole lot of shit going on.
When did you do the field work picking berries and stuff? Field work?

Yeah, that's when I was about six or seven, eight, nine years old. Where would you pick berries? I went through Hammond, Independent, Impostor Tool, Hall Bennett, Emet, Serento, Velma, Shiloh, Spencefield, Independent, Mopo, No showing off.
Well hey, who'd you work for then? This was when you were kids?
Well you were just working for people who were on the farms, you know.
Who'd take you out there?
Well they send trucks to pick you out there. How many hands they would need, they would come in and sit on the corner and ask for hands.
You mean somebody would drive a truck like in your neighborhood or something?

Well you didn't never know where the truck drivers come from either. I mean they would have to make a buck too. All they did would haul you there. And after that you may have never seen them no more. Their job was to get you to your designation. Uh huh. Wow.

So uh, after the CCC camp, like what did you do? Well I came back out here. And then you must have started playing music again. Yeah I did. Did you start playing? And whenever I could, but most of the time I was gambling, you know.
I made more money than I did. Gambling?
What'd you like? What was your favorite? My favorite game was Coon Camp.
But I played checkers.
Coon Camp. Well no, you gotta explain that to me. Coon Camp? Yeah, what's that? What is it?
Well, you heard of P-Knuckle. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Pity Pat. Right. Black Jack. Right. You heard of Koch.
Skin. No, no, never heard of that.
Well if you haven't heard of Skin you haven't heard of Coon Camp.
You heard of Pity Pat? Yeah, well how is it played?

How is it played? Well it's so long. Pity Pat is a short way of pronouncing Coon Camp. The only thing, if you're playing Pity Pat you use one chord against the other. Coon Camp you have to use two against one. To use this one queen you have to have two queens in your hand. Right. So if this is queen of heart, you need queen of diamonds or queen of speed or queen of diamonds or queen of club or any two queens. Right. But by this being queen of heart, if you've got jack of heart and seven of hearts you can also use this queen of heart. Right. Or if you've got the jack of hearts and the king of hearts you can split and use this queen.
It's just you've got to see it to understand it. Well it gives me some idea.
Yes. It's just a long way of playing Pity Pat but you can play in three different ways in Coon Camp. You can play one suit against the other if it's in hearts or clubs or diamonds or speeds.
Right. So could you do any tricks? Did you do any card tricks? I bet you could do some 90s. I see it.
I was a professional card player.

He supported during like the ten or fifteen years but in the fifties and all when you know he wasn't playing much music before I met him in 70 or whenever it was. He supported himself and went back to playing cards all during that period.
So you're that good at it. You're that good at playing cards. You could support yourself at it.
I'm good enough not to lose. Nah.
So where would you play? Where were some good places to play back then? Well, well, what clubs?
And didn't everybody play with you that knowed me? You know what I mean?
Well there's some professional, I know there's some gambling houses around.
Just the guys that's daring, that don't believe. Those are the only guys that I could, you know.
Yeah, well anybody who really knows what they're doing, you know. Doesn't want to come up against some people.
I had a lot of channelers. He doesn't want to come up against somebody who's got it. All I had to do was have a bankroll and that, if you could get a bankroll, you had it made.
You had a bankroll?
Yeah. Anybody that knew me would put up a bankroll, you know. Uh huh. I wasn't worried about the money.
So where'd you find these people? They'd find me. Did they come to your house? I was a champ. Did they come to your house or was there some illegal club?
If you were looking for a fight and the champ had the belt, should he look for you or should you look for him? Oh, he'll look for you.
Yeah, that's right. I'm trying to find out if there were any illegal gambling places. I knew there were a few. There were a bunch. Well, really. Ain't no places.
The only place that the gambling was going on was illegal gambling places. No, but there were some specific ones. Yeah, there were a bunch of specific ones in the backs of the bar rooms. Yeah.

Well, I know the Big 25 used to have them. Yeah. The Big 25 always had something illegal going on. There was some other place. There was... I'm trying to think of the name of it. There was one uptown, I know, and I can't think of the name of it.
Yeah, well, I wouldn't call the name of it. There was a place on Oak Street, I think.
Yeah, well... Used to have a guy at my house.
I don't know if it'd be wise to call their names, you know.
